idiom_name: second translation unit implementing the service header (link seam, ld --wrap, or CMock-generated stubs)
implementation_notes: C has no interfaces and no dynamic dispatch, so the classic stub class is replaced by a second implementation of the same function set: link stub_tax.c instead of client_tax.c into the test binary, or keep one binary and redirect individual symbols with GNU ld's -Wl,--wrap=symbol, where every reference to symbol resolves to __wrap_symbol and the original stays reachable as __real_symbol. CMock takes the next step and generates that translation unit from the service header, which keeps the stub's signatures in step with the contract at build time. Choose the hand-written seam while only a few functions need canned values, and generate stubs once hand-maintained signatures start drifting.
pitfalls: A seam that never fires is the classic C failure: -Wl,--wrap only redirects undefined references resolved at link time, so a static function, an inlined call or an LTO-merged definition silently keeps calling the real code and the test passes for the wrong reason.
There is no instance to own the stub's state: fixture data in file-scope statics survives between tests unless each test resets it explicitly.
The stub must match the header exactly (const qualifiers, pointer-to-struct versus by-value, calling convention); a mismatch links and then reads uninitialised memory.

variants.name: CMock-generated mock/stub from the service header
variants.implementation_notes: CMock parses the C header and emits the stand-in translation unit together with call recording and expectation APIs, so the stub's signatures follow the contract automatically and no hand-written glue is needed. Prefer it when the header is the contract and the test build already runs Ceedling; the price is a Ruby-based codegen step in the build and an expectation API that tempts tests into over-specifying calls.
pitfalls: The header becomes the only truth: a header that drifted from the wire contract produces a stub that agrees with the header and not with the service.
Expectation macros record exact arguments and order, so unrelated client refactors fail tests that only ever needed canned data.
